items.title: Raleigh's housing reforms helped ease rents, Pew study finds
items.description: For years, homebuilding leaders have argued that the most effective way to lower housing costs is to build more, and that cities that adopt pro-housing reforms will be rewarded with greater supply and more attainable housing. New research from The Pew Charitable Trusts shows what happened when Raleigh, N.C., followed that playbook. Following the pandemic, Raleigh overhauled its zoning and land use laws to make building easier, Pew found. The result was a building boom, particularly for the townhomes and apartments the city's earlier rules constrained. This uptick in homebuilding made renting more affordable in North Carolina’s capital city, especially for middle-income households and younger residents. The report highlights how adding new housing supply at scale can improve housing affordability, echoing similar impacts that followed concerted rezoning efforts in Minneapolis-St. Paul, Minn., and Austin, Texas. The same dynamic is playing out across the Sun Belt, where many of the nation’s fastest-growing metros also have some of the loosest zoning rules, and where rents and home prices have dropped more dramatically than anywhere else in the country. Raleigh’s post-COVID zoning reforms Raleigh didn't rely on a single fix to make building housing easier. Its reforms combined a rewrite of its form-based code, an end to parking minimums, denser building near transit and a housing bond to support affordable housing. “Of all of the drivers of housing costs – population growth, an influx of high-income earners, high land costs and high construction costs – we have the most agency and direct control over restrictive zoning regulations,” Patrick Young, Raleigh’s planning and development director, said in a statement. Allowing more missing middle housing Raleigh's 2021 zoning reform, which expanded the city’s already-established form-based code, opened the door to more "missing middle" housing. It did so by replacing units-per-acre caps with physical standards such as lot size, yards, and building height. The changes legalized duplexes, triplexes and quadplexes in more residential districts and expanded where townhomes can be built. Under the new form-based code, further refined in 2022, builders can now construct small apartment buildings and tiny houses with up to two dwelling units on compact infill lots. As a result, builders can now construct missing middle housing in more of Raleigh's neighborhoods, a shift that Pew links to better affordability for middle-income and younger residents. Reforming transit-oriented development and parking requirements Raleigh eliminated its citywide parking minimums in 2022. That allowed developers to fit more housing units on each property and, in some cases, spared them the expense of building costly parking structures, which can often make a project too costly to pursue. The city also spurred housing growth by allowing taller, denser buildings near major transit corridors. Transit Overlay District zones allowed for an extra story along Bus Rapid Transit corridors, extending half a mile along some local bus routes. Additionally, a density bonus allows developers to exceed height limits by up to 50% if at least 20% of the extra units are designated as affordable, below-market units. Approving housing bonds to incentivize affordable housing The City of Raleigh approved an $80 million housing bond in 2020 that is projected to create at least 700 affordable homes, fund homebuyer assistance and help homeowners with home repairs. About $14 million has already gone to four developments totaling more than 240 units, while another $24 million in gap financing will back over 470 additional units, more than 90% of which will be affordable to households earning 60% of area median income or less. How these reforms contributed to moderated rent growth Between 2021 and 2024, Raleigh added 16,884 housing units, growing its housing stock by 7.7%, even as the city’s population grew by 5.8% over the same period. Raleigh's housing growth also outpaced the state (5.7%) and national (3.2%) rates during that period. Of the 16,884 units added, roughly 2,000, or 12%, were affordable to households earning 80% or less of area median income (AMI), with Raleigh's housing bond funds helping support their development. Density bonuses contributed about 200 of those affordable units, accounting for 10% of the total. Additionally, Raleigh’s code changes intentionally shifted a large share of production away from detached single-family homes toward townhomes, duplexes and tiny homes. Since 2021, the city has issued more than twice as many townhouse permits as in 2015 to 2020, and has permitted more than 200 duplex units and over 200 accessory dwelling units (ADUs). As a result, average monthly rents rose at only half the national pace and fell in real, inflation-adjusted terms. Pew’s analysis estimates inflation-adjusted rents declined 15% from 2022 to 2025, and, as of 2025, the income needed to afford the city’s median rent dropped from 79% of AMI to 65%. Raleigh's experience mirrors a wider trend among fast-growing Sun Belt markets, where less restrictive zoning and fewer barriers to housing development have supported greater housing production and helped moderate housing costs. The South accounted for more than half of all U.S. housing starts between 2021 and 2025, while Sun Belt markets continue to lead the nation in rent and home price declines. According to Yardi Matrix's October 2026 multifamily report , rents fell year over year in 12 major US markets. The Sun Belt accounted for ten of those, led by Austin, Houston, Nashville, Tampa and Phoenix. The for-sale market shows a similar pattern, with home prices dropping disproportionately in the Sun Belt while climbing in the Northeast and Midwest. Related More: Affordability Homebuilders

items.title: City Backs Mixed-Use Plan At Underutilized North Philly Amtrak Stop
items.description: Philadelphia officials and developers are joining forces to seek federal funding for a mixed-use development around an underutilized transit hub. Wikimedia Commons/Pi.1415926535 Shift Capital and Essence Development, owners of 10 mostly vacant acres near the North Philadelphia Amtrak station, are looking to obtain low-cost, long-term financing from the U.S. Department of Transportation to build a transit-oriented district. The city is now helping advance predevelopment work necessary to obtain that financing. On Thursday, the Office of Transportation and Infrastructure Systems released a request for proposals for a firm to conduct development services. The firm would receive up to $595K for the contract, which will be centered on ensuring the proposal is eligible to receive the DOT financing. The city says it will make streetscape improvements and design and placemaking decisions while compiling land and facilitating the entitlement process. “The North Station District represents the most important economic opportunity in Philadelphia in a generation,” Shift CEO Brian Murray said in a March press release . While the proposed development site is less than half a mile from the Allegheny stop on the Broad Street line and served by three SEPTA commuter rail lines and four high-frequency bus routes, the Amtrak station has fewer than 300 daily riders, according to the RFP. The document attributes this to low residential and employment density around the site straddling the Allegheny West and Glenwood neighborhoods. It also frames incentivizing economic development as a way to promote equity in the area, which has a 22% unemployment rate and a 46% poverty rate. This section of the city was included in Pennsylvania’s submissions for the new version of the federal opportunity zone tax incentive program that goes into effect at the start of next year. “The absence of dense, mixed-use, transit-supportive development limits ridership growth, constrains access to jobs and education for nearby residents, and suppresses broader economic activity in surrounding neighborhoods,” the RFP says. The initial contract is set to start in April 2027 and last one year, but the city will have the right to extend it for four additional years. The transit infrastructure moved thousands of people every day during North Philly’s heyday in the early 20th century, according to the March release from Shift announcing a partnership at the site with Essence and Temple University . The school is not mentioned in the RFP. Applications must be submitted by 5 p.m. on Jan. 20. To qualify, applicants must also attend a preproposal Zoom meeting at noon on Dec. 14. items.title: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul Signs New Private Listings Bill
items.description: New York has signed a new private listings bill, which means that properties will be required to be visible to the public as they hit the market unless the seller signs an informed opt-out consent. Late last week, Gov. Kathy Hochul signed the Fair and Transparent Real Estate Listing Act . The language of the bill requires that real estate listings be marketed in "at least one other publication, platform or website that does not require payment" or for the consumer to work with the brokerage for access. This follows a quick path through the state's Legislature, which approved the act in a noncontroversial vote in June. The New York State Association of Realtors® strongly supports the bill. This becomes the latest crackdown on private listings, where a real estate agent markets a property to a limited list of buyers before making it public. Fair housing advocates say private listings raise discrimination concerns. One study from Bright MLS found private listings take longer to sell and don't guarantee more money. The listing must be accessible to the general public, "without limitation to a particular brokerage, franchise or select group of licenses." Also, there can't be restrictions on some or all of the details in the listing, according to the language of the bill. The bill doesn't require a seller or lister to hold open houses or public showings if it violates any state or federal laws related to health and safety. And sellers can opt out, by signing a form that explicitly warns them that the listing will have limited visibility and possible impact on the price they get. New York can punish violators with a fine of up to $5,000 and suspension or revocation of their real estate license. Earlier this year, the state saw its inventory of homes for sale fall to a 30-year low . Private listings debate Washington and Connecticut have passed similar laws this year. Each has generally similar language in their bills, which also allow for opt-outs. A study from Zillow found the sales price of private listings was 1.3% less than comparable sales on the multiple listing service, costing the seller an average of $4,230 per sale. ( Realtor.com® recently struck an agreement with Zillow to show preview listings from brokers who participate in Zillow’s preview program, in an effort to boost market transparency.) Compass Inc., the real estate brokerage giant which has defended its use of private listings, said its recently unveiled See It First listings strategy complies with the law. It launched that program in September, which gives early access to homes that will soon be listed on the public market. Users don't need to work with a Compass agent to use it. "New York’s new law preserves homeowners’ right to choose how they market their homes, including the ability to use a See It First strategy to test pricing and gauge demand," a Compass spokesperson said. "See It First early access homes comply with the new law and continue to give sellers flexibility in how and when they bring their homes to market." Loading... Compass CEO Robert Reffkin has defended the company's listings strategy. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images New York has long struggled with housing affordability. The Realtor.com State-by-State Housing Report Card gave the Empire State an F, the lowest rating possible. Hochul has emphasized affordability concerns and made a deregulation push to make home construction easier. “My administration is focused on making New York more affordable and liveable for every New Yorker regardless of age or income, and housing is central to that goal,” Hochul said last week. Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

items.title: BTR sector fears Treasury rules move the goal line on investor ban
items.description: Earlier this year, build-to-rent projects secured some notable exemptions from the institutional investor ban included in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. However, while the industry still doesn't know exactly what the final rules will look like, it just moved a step closer to finding out. Monday marked the end of the U.S. Department of the Treasury 's public comment period on its proposed rules for BTR exemptions from the institutional investor ban . Although ROAD explicitly exempted BTR from the ban, some of the proposed rules and language Treasury released in October have left the industry uneasy and unsure of where it stands. BTR developers and operators say this uncertainty continues to suppress capital flowing into new projects, a trend they expect to continue until the federal government clarifies the rules. Last month, Treasury released a notice of proposed rulemaking detailing how it would implement the institutional investor ban while protecting BTR communities. The proposed rules would exempt newly built, never-owner-occupied BTR communities if an investor buys them within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy and uses them only as rentals. Treasury would also exempt communities that include both rental and for-sale homes, allowing builders to sell the rental portion to large institutional investors while marketing the remaining homes to individual buyers. The proposals additionally call for allowing transfers of existing BTR communities between large institutional investors and keeping the renovate-to-rent exemption. Although the rules appear to protect BTR, industry leaders say the finer details leave several concerns unresolved. “If you read the law as a layman, you’d say, ‘all right, built-to-rent is carved out.’ But then you get this rulemaking, and it’s like you have to pat your belly and tap your head and hop on one foot for the built-to-rent to not be banned,” Sean Dobson, chairman, CEO and CIO at The Amherst Group , said in an interview with HousingWire TBD . Over the last month, Treasury received more than 450 letters with questions and concerns concerning its proposed rulemakings. HousingWire TBD reviewed 10 of those letters, from high-profile BTR developers and operators and leading organizations that advocate on behalf of the rental housing industry, including: National Apartments Association (NAA) and National Multifamily Housing Council (NMHC) National Rental Home Council (NRHC) Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) Up for Growth Action Berkadia LGI Homes Landmark Properties Quinn Residences AHV Communities A coalition of 12 developers, including Greystar and Brookfield Residential These letters detailed the outstanding concerns that the industry still has concerning how Treasury will enforce ROAD. With the institutional investor ban set to take effect on January 7, Treasury has several weeks to finalize and release the rules that BTR operators will have to follow. Until then, the industry has to wait and see whether, and how, those concerns are addressed. The 18-month certificate-of-occupancy deadline The chief concern among BTR developers, operators and advocates is the proposed requirement that institutional investors purchase BTR communities within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy (CO). Under the proposed framework, if a developer fails to sell a community by that deadline, they may lose the ability to do so altogether. That proposal matters because many BTR developers, much like multifamily developers, rely on selling their communities after completion and stabilization to make a profit and move on to their next project. Richard Ross, CEO at Quinn Residences , argued that the 18-month window is far too limiting. A community may still be under development and lease-up after the first homes receive a CO, so 18 months will almost certainly run out before the full community is ready to sell. “To build and stabilize a new community takes about 30 months. If I start receiving certificates of occupancy at month 15, I may not receive the final CO for the last home until month 28 or 29. I need enough time to complete and stabilize the entire community before selling it,” Ross said in an interview. The letters that HousingWire TBD reviewed unanimously opposed the proposed 18-month window. Just like Ross, industry groups argued that the deadline does not align with how rental communities are developed, leased up, financed and sold. The letter signed by a coalition of 12 BTR developers led by Greystar and Brookfield Residential argued that the deadline would create uncertainty for projects that may not be sold until years after construction. The letter further argued the restrictions would continue to affect financing decisions for future projects. “A smaller potential buyer pool reduces liquidity and creates greater uncertainty regarding terminal value,” the letter read. Additionally, the groups argued that Treasury must protect long-term institutional owners' ability to purchase BTR communities. Otherwise, the federal government would undermine the industry. “If large institutional investors cannot purchase horizontal multifamily communities (which individual families cannot), the values of those properties will fall and new construction and necessary maintenance and reinvestment will slow,” MBA’s letter read. To address this, NAA and NMHC, two of the largest rental housing advocacy organizations, requested that Treasury eliminate the deadline or replace it with a provision that institutional investors can purchase BTR communities directly from the builder or developer responsible for construction. Quinn Residences, AHV Communities and LGI Homes also requested that Treasury remove or substantially extend the deadline. LGI Homes also emphasized the need for production homebuilders to retain the option of renting homes that have not sold. items.title: FHFA maps out FICO 10T rollout with broad eligibility by late 2028
items.description: The Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the FICO 10T credit score model for use by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac . It also released an implementation road map that would make FICO 10T broadly eligible and retire Classic FICO by September 2028. The staged rollout, announced Tuesday, mirrors the VantageScore 4.0 timeline and is meant to give lenders, mortgage insurers and loan origination system providers time to analyze historic FICO 10T data, rework pricing and risk models, and update technology before a full transition, according to the agency. "The timeline below prepares lenders, mortgage insurers and loan origination system providers for the final step in credit score modernization: lender choice between FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0," the agency said. At the Federal Housing Administration (FHA), VantageScore 4.0 and FICO 10T are expected to go live alongside the existing Classic FICO in January. Bob Broeksmit , president and CEO of the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), issued a statement of support following the announcement. “We welcome this milestone as it moves us closer to the industry's and FHFA’s goal of transitioning to true competition with two modernized credit score models," Broeksmit said. "We appreciate FHFA's desire to provide a clear and transparent roadmap for this process. Given the industry’s experience with the just-completed adoption of VantageScore 4.0, MBA will work with FHFA and industry stakeholders to expedite the implementation timeline responsibly. "MBA and its members will continue to engage with FHFA to establish meaningful competition for both credit scoring and credit reporting. Continued reforms to end the tri-merge requirement will further improve our credit reporting system and lower costs for borrowers. Today’s announcement is a critical next step." Staged rollout The FHFA initially validated both FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0 for use at the government-sponsored (GSEs) enterprises in October 2022. In July 2026, Fannie and Freddie released historical performance data for FICO 10T along with additional VantageScore 4.0 data, a key prerequisite for lenders and investors to back-test new score models and recalibrate credit policy. A FICO 10T pilot is expected to begin around December 2027. In this “launch and refine” phase, lenders will deliver a subset of loans underwritten with FICO 10T while FHFA, the GSEs and industry stakeholders monitor data quality, pricing and delivery performance. Based on pilot results, FHFA expects upfront pricing grids and private mortgage insurer eligibility requirements, or PMIERs, to be updated to reflect the new score model. That step will be critical for secondary market execution and risk transfer structures that currently rely on Classic FICO. A limited FICO 10T rollout is targeted for April 2028, followed by a scale-up and transition phase that leads to broad eligibility around September 2028. During this final stage, FHFA plans to confirm industry readiness, fully implement Uniform Loan Delivery Dataset (ULDD) Phase 5, expand FICO 10T use across GSE channels and retire Classic FICO. FHFA emphasized that dates after November 2026 are targets and are subject to change. Pricing dynamics In October, Fair Isaac Corp. said it will hold its wholesale mortgage price at $10 for a bundle of its credit scores for lenders and brokers enrolled in its Preferred Program. The $10 price is available through participating tri-merge credit report resellers to lenders that commit to FICO under the program. It covers both Classic FICO, which has been the mortgage standard for nearly three decades, and FICO Score 10T, the company’s trended-data model. FICO is also preparing a new subscription-based pricing model for mortgage credit scores in 2027, sources told HousingWire . VantageScore 4.0, by comparison, has been offered at 99 cents per score , or at no additional charge when purchased alongside a FICO score through Equifax , Experian and TransUnion , which jointly own VantageScore. Bank of America Global Research , using data from Recursion , found that more than 170 lenders now pull VantageScore 4.0. Despite that breadth of use, only a small share of conventional loans are actually priced with VantageScore 4.0. In October, 20% of issuance reported a VantageScore 4.0, yet only about 8% of total issuance used the score model for pricing, according to the research. Editor's note: This story was updated with a statement from the MBA. Related More: Credit Score FHFA FICO

items.title: FHFA raises conforming loan limit to $855,400 in 2027
items.description: The baseline conforming loan limit will rise 2.71% in 2027 to $855,400 for one-unit properties in most parts of the country, according to the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA). Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will be authorized to buy loans up to that balance in the vast majority of U.S. counties. The $855,400 cap is an increase of $22,650 from 2026 and reflects slower home price growth tied to a weaker housing market and higher-for-longer mortgage rates . The annual adjustment was 3.25% last year and above 5% in each of the prior two years. Under the Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008 (HERA), the national “ceiling” for high-cost areas is set at 150% of the baseline. For 2027, that ceiling will be $1,283,100 for one-unit properties in markets where 115% of the local median home value exceeds the baseline limit. Conforming caps first surpassed $1 million in these high-cost areas in 2022. Special statutory provisions apply in Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands. In these areas, the 2027 baseline loan limit for one-unit properties will be $1,283,100, while the ceiling will be $1,924,650. “Due to rising home values, the CLL will be higher in all but 24 U.S. counties or county equivalents,” the FHFA said in a statement. How FHFA set the 2027 limit Each November, FHFA publishes new conforming loan limits for the coming year. Increases resumed in 2016, after home prices returned to pre-Great Recession levels, a condition required by HERA. The statute also prevents the ceiling from declining in years when home prices fall; the cap only moves higher when national prices increase year over year. This year’s adjustment is tied to FHFA’s third-quarter 2026 House Price Index (HPI), which tracks changes in average U.S. home values over the prior four quarters. Nominal, seasonally adjusted, expanded-data HPI showed house prices rose 2.72% on average between the third quarters of 2025 and 2026, essentially matching the 2.71% rise in the baseline conforming loan limit. The new limits expand the amount of mortgage debt that can qualify for conventional financing backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac . Loans above FHFA’s limits are classified as jumbos, a segment still dominated by banks and portfolio lenders that set their own credit standards and capital requirements. Mortgage lenders once again anticipated FHFA’s announcement and raised their internal conforming loan limits ahead of the official release to compete for volume. But they were conservative. Rocket Mortgage was an early mover, lifting its conforming loan limit to $845,000 for single-family homes in 48 states in September. CrossCountry Mortgage adopted the same level. Pennymac set its internal limit at $850,000, while United Wholesale Mortgage increased its one-unit cap for conventional and Department of Veterans Affairs loans to $847,440. items.title: Mortgage rates whiplash is in full effect, with jumbo loans shedding 25 bps this week
items.description: The seesaw pattern for mortgage rates that's been the story for much of the second half of 2026 reared its head again this week as rates for major loan types declined, reversing some of the increases from prior weeks. At HousingWire 's Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, rates for 30-year conforming loans averaged 7.53% — down 5 basis points from a week ago. Rates for 30-year loans through the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) dropped 7 bps to 7.30%, while rates for 30-year jumbo loans plummeted 25 bps to 7.62%. Rates in the mid-7% range continue to weigh on homebuyer demand and affordability metrics. Last week's application index from the Mortgage Bankers Association showed that total applications were down 5% on a weekly basis. MBA data released Tuesday found that affordability is about 8% weaker than a year ago , even though it improved slightly from September to October. “Higher mortgage rates weighed on application activity last week, with the 30-year fixed rate rising to 7.35%. Purchase applications were down 18% from a year ago, reflecting continued affordability challenges and softer homebuyer demand. The direction of mortgage rates in the coming weeks will be key to the housing market’s momentum heading into 2027,” MBA president and CEO Bob Broeksmit said in a statement. Dan Ribler , vice president of capital markets and strategy at national reverse mortgage lender Longbridge Financial , said that the October jobs report should've sent rates higher . Nonfarm payrolls increased by 165,000 positions last month and the unemployment rate remained steady at 4.1%, indicative of today's healthier labor market conditions in relation to 2025. Ribler noted that the jobless rate has been below 5% every month since September 2021, unemployment claims are lower than a year ago and the Federal Reserve 's "own description is the labor market is very strong." But strong employment trends have been overshadowed by stubborn inflation , which continues to run well above the central bank's 2% annualized target. "Inflation has been above 2% year over year 57 months in a row," Ribler remarked. "The Fed has, by the way, under this administration, reiterated the 2% hurdle and that they're going to be tough on inflation. They're certainly talking the hawk talk, saying we're going to keep inflation under 2%. "But man, I don't know about you, if my kid breaks curfew 57 nights in a row — and I say I'm going to punish you one of these times and I never do anything about it — at some point, he stops believing me, right?" Inflation is likely to prompt the Fed to raise rates next month. The CME Group 's FedWatch tool reveals that a 25-bps hike in December is all but certain, with 96% of interest rate traders saying that the federal funds rate will rise to a range of 4% to 4.25%. It was last at that level in September 2025. Silver linings are hard to identify Much of the housing and mortgage industry headlines in the past week have cast a shadow over any potential market improvements in 2027. Selma Hepp , chief economist at Cotality , said in a statement that existing home sales have fallen to their lowest level since August 2010. She also pointed to a Realtor.com analysis, which found that the typical repeat buyer will pay about $1,100 more per month if they choose to sell and move. "A meaningful housing recovery requires rates to come down and, importantly, stay down long enough to improve affordability and unlock turnover," Hepp said. "Until then, the adjustment is likely to come through weaker sales and softer home prices rather than widespread homeowner distress. "The number worth writing is the $1,100. That's the jump in monthly payment a typical repeat buyer takes on just to move house. It's the clearest explanation yet of why nobody is selling." New home sales have been equally grim, with September's seasonally adjusted annual rate of 676,000 sales representing a 5.3% decline from a year ago. Higher rates have also prompted homebuilders to remain cautious about creating more supply, with U.S. Census Bureau figures showing that single-family housing starts were down 3.2% year over year in September. Monthly gains in total starts were largely tied to the multifamily sector. "Challenging affordability has been weighing on the resale market. Newly pending sales fell 17% in October, the largest year-over-year drop since 2023," Zillow senior economist Kenny Lee said in a statement. "Single-family homebuilders have been navigating the same challenge. While homebuilders have been adapting to the softer market by offering concessions and building smaller homes, the 2027 spring home-shopping season could see a slow start as buyer demand continues to wane." The relative lack of sales has weighed on mortgage origination volumes, with ATTOM data for the third quarter of 2026 showing that the roughly 730,000 purchase loans closed during that period were the lowest figure for any third quarter in 14 years. Refinance activity was also bleak, with the roughly 561,000 refis in Q3 down 19% year over year. Refi lending was down from Q2 2026 in nearly 90% of the metro areas analyzed by ATTOM, with the largest declines in major metros like San Jose, San Francisco , Dallas, Austin and Louisville, Kentucky. items.title: Maryland Life Sciences Players Urge Coordination To Spur Growth
items.description: Suburban Maryland’s life sciences corridor has some of the most important pieces of the research and development puzzle already built in: the National Institutes of Health , the Food and Drug Administration and a deep bench of research and talent from universities like Johns Hopkins University and the University of Maryland. But more coordination is needed to fully harness the power of those scientific assets for the region’s growth and economy, panelists at Bisnow ’s Mid-Atlantic Life Sciences and Biotech Summit said this month. “This is our time to come together and to put ourselves on the map, and we do that by producing the science, by supporting our startups and by encouraging innovation and commercialization right here in this region,” Ecphora Capital Managing Partner Deborah Hemingway said onstage at the Bethesda Marriott. Bisnow/Emily Wishingrad Montgomery County Economic Development Corp.'s Prayas Neupane, Universities at Shady Grove’s Anne Khademian, Ecphora Capital’s Deborah Hemingway, Association of University Research Parks’ Brian Darmody and Stein Sperling’s Andrew Schwartz There is inherently a pipeline that those in the industry call “bench-to-bedside,” whereby basic research produces insight that then leads to real-world uses like patient treatment and diagnostics. But panelists said creating infrastructure around those collaborative efforts, concepts like innovation districts or centers of excellence, can boost the region from an economic development standpoint. “It's a collective effort, and we need to be thinking strategically around how do we market ourselves as a region, and how do we attract the companies that would have never thought about being here in that sense,” said Prayas Neupane, Montgomery County Economic Development Corp.’s director of economic development. From a real estate perspective, the idea would be to build structural hubs that can collate players across the life sciences spectrum — from academic institutions to private companies to hospital systems. In addition to enabling various players to collaborate scientifically, they would also help attract more companies and investment and provide a branding advantage for the region. “So why couldn't we create a Purple Line innovation corridor north and south, so you can actually bring together from a marketing standpoint FDA and NIH and College Park and NOAA and all of these assets,” Association of University Research Parks Chief Strategy Officer Brian Darmody said. The long-awaited Purple Line, which connects New Carrollton to the east and downtown Bethesda to the west, is tentatively set to open late next year. Darmody noted that there are three Maryland medical schools. In addition to Hopkins and UMD, there is also the federal Uniformed Health Sciences University in Bethesda. “We have these assets that are just sub-optimized because we don't have enough awareness of them, and I think if we collectively pull them together, that will make this region much stronger,” he said. Bisnow/Emily Wishingrad ATCC’s Rupali Lach, CannonDesign’s Charu McDermott, Whiting-Turner’s Colin Regan, Merrick and Co.'s Patrick Conley, Athari BioSciences Inc.’s Susan Mitchell, Sapient Biotech’s Bibhash Mukhopadhyay and Scheer Partners’ Matthew Brady Some efforts to create these kinds of innovation hubs in the region are underway. A 14-acre life sciences district next to the North Bethesda Metro station is in the works, set to be anchored by the University of Maryland’s Institute for Health Computing. The Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority selected Hines as the developer for the project last year. MCB Real Estate , which is building Viva White Oak, a $2.8B mixed-use development next to the FDA, envisions 3M SF of office space with a focus on the life science industries . Onstage, Darmody called the Viva White Oak effort “needed,” but he said the county still has to be working toward attracting companies to fill that planned development. “Somebody, a new intermediary, whether it's Montgomery County EDC or a new regional enterprise, has to provide the strategy and the facilities and the financing to get more of that in the private sector,” he said. Panelists said the field of quantum sciences could be an opportunity to create a specialized hub in the region, given its preexisting strength in the space. But it's easier said than done, panelists said, as these efforts require the necessary coordination, funding, political will and patience from public and private partners to see them through. “We need to do a better job of communicating and really talking, and then doing, doing the real work,” Athari BioSciences Inc. CEO and founder Susan Mitchell said. “It's hard work. It's hard. It's long, it's tedious, and it's costly, but if we want to be the center of excellence, because the mid-Atlantic region is ripe for it, we have the tools, we have the people, we just need to do it. Stop talking about it and do it.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Brian Darmody , Deborah Hemingway , Food and Drug Administration , National Institutes of Health , Patrick Conley , Prayas Neupane , Purple Line , Susan Mitchell

items.title: Research Triangle's Biomanufacturing Surge Is Luring More Companies
items.description: Ongoing investment in biomanufacturing across the Research Triangle is drawing more companies to the region and boosting the market’s research and development sector. Large pharmaceutical companies, including AbbVie and Novartis, have committed hundreds of millions of dollars in the past year to expand their manufacturing operations in the region. Those investments are also attracting smaller biomanufacturing firms to the area, panelists said at Bisnow ’s Research Triangle Life Sciences Summit in Raleigh this month. “The ecosystem has been buoyed up by the large groups that have come here, and it has become very ripe and fertile ground for the smaller, medium-sized companies coming behind it,” Jonathon Keener, a partner at Helix Ventures, said at the Brier Creek Country Club in Raleigh. “That's what we're most excited about because that diversifies our economy here.” Wikimedia/Abhiram Juvvadi In January, contract development and manufacturing organization Alcami paid $6.7M for a 37K SF biologics lab facility in Durham. In April, pharmaceutical supplier NewLife Medicals expanded into Efland with its $4.8M acquisition of a 28K SF flex warehouse. And Ypsomed, a midsized Swiss medical technology company, is building its first U.S. manufacturing facility with a $200M investment in Holly Springs, with plans to open by the end of 2027. Shifting trade policies and increased demand for U.S.-based production have prompted the life sciences industry to put more of its focus on manufacturing. Manufacturing has become “a national priority,” sparking new demand from life sciences companies for “facilities that can support process development, pilot production and commercial-scale manufacturing,” Tyler Grimshaw, principal of architecture and engineering firm EwingCole , told Bisnow ahead of the event . Raleigh-Durham’s life sciences market is showing signs of stabilization, according to a Cushman & Wakefield third-quarter report . Nearly 2.4M SF of new life sciences space has delivered since 2021. In the third quarter, vacancy in the market fell to 26.4% from 28% in the same quarter of 2025, reaching the lowest level in two years. This year, absorption turned positive again following occupancy losses in 2024. Pexels/Pavel Danilyuk The Research Triangle has seen a slew of large biomanufacturing real estate investments over the past year. Last month, diagnostic imaging company Bracco Imaging announced a $230M investment in a manufacturing facility in Sanford, just south of the Triangle. In April, AbbVie announced a $1.4B investment to build a 185-acre pharmaceutical manufacturing campus in Durham, with completion slated for the end of 2028. And in May, Novartis announced plans to add a new $220M facility , spanning 56K SF in Morrisville, part of a $23B U.S. manufacturing and R&D commitment . After a period of large-footprint commitments, smaller biomanufacturing companies are also coming to the Triangle. “There's been a slowdown in some of the larger users — and there's definitely been an uptick in the more medium- to small-range-size users,” said Carolyn Coia, vice president of real estate at Research Triangle Park . Part of that uptick is also due to the Research Triangle’s talent pool, flowing from North Carolina State University, Duke University and other universities in the area. “What North Carolina is great at is producing the future employees” for pharmaceutical companies, said Michael Morgan, managing director of tenant representation at JLL. Life sciences employment in the Research Triangle grew 21% from 2020 through 2025, reaching more than 58,000 workers across more than 650 companies, according to a 2026 Wake County Economic Development report . The region's employment concentration sits at 2.64 times the national average, outpacing national growth benchmarks, the report said. Panelists expect continued life sciences growth as regional talent keeps bringing in companies. “Once they come with their first initial investment, putting their toe in the pond, they realize what that talent can do for them, and they quickly double down,” Keener said. items.title: Capital Is There, But Dutch Real Estate Needs Stability, Tax Relief And Power To Unlock It
items.description: A stable, dependable government with predictable policies, lower transfer tax and more solutions for grid congestion. That is what Dutch real estate is asking Sinterklaas for this year, according to speakers at Bisnow ’s Netherlands State of the Market event, held at KIT, formerly known as the Royal Tropical Institute, in Amsterdam. Bisnow/Mike Phillips APG's Robert-Jan Footse, Vesteda's Astrid Schlüter, Hines' Jan Hein Tiedema, CBRE IM's Jan-Willem Bastijn and ABS Real Estate Finance's Bert van den Hoek While some of these issues may be a bit trickier to overcome than others, speakers were adamant that addressing them would help bring capital back into the market. Money is there, and investors are keen to deploy it under the right conditions. “In January our outlook of the Dutch market was fairly positive, and that’s what we saw in the first and second quarter: a lot of traction in the residential market, mainly driven by Dutch institutional investors and family offices,” said Jan Hein Tiedema, head of the Netherlands at Hines , which manages $91B (€83B) in assets across approximately 30 countries. Commercial real estate investment volume reached €7B in the first half of 2026, up 36% on the same period last year, according to CBRE Netherlands. It is forecast to hit €15B for the full year, which would represent a 15% jump for the full year. However, the market shifted after summer, and not necessarily for the better. “With interest rates rising, I see many deals postponed, delayed and renegotiated,” Tiedema said. “We’re facing it ourselves on the selling side as well as on the buying side.” That same cautious approach is evident in capital allocation, with investors becoming increasingly selective about how and where they allocate money. Hines had been attempting to sell a residential asset in Amsterdam in September that was initially perceived as a “great deal, with plenty of appetite,” Tiedema said. However, the bids received were below expectations, leading Hines to pull the sale. With interest rates likely to rise before they fall in the eurozone, investors are relying on income returns to make money, and rents are rising in all sectors for good assets because of limited new supply. So the question arises: Where is capital still going in the Netherlands? Robert-Jan Foortse , head of European property investments at APG , one of the world’s largest pension investors, said the company had committed about €3B to its residential development partner platforms, including a tie-up with CBRE IM . “Of that €3B, we’ve allocated roughly €1.5B to actual projects. The NAV at the moment is only €500M, so we have some way to go,” Foortse said, adding that it was looking at forward funding and turnkey development. The Netherlands is grappling with an acute housing shortage, which is estimated to be at 384,000 homes, or 4.6% of the housing stock, according to the Ministry of Housing and Spatial Planning. As such, many domestic investors are investing in residential property. But just because there is a lack of supply doesn’t make it a good investment opportunity, Foortse said. APG has a mandate to invest capital in the Dutch residential market, particularly new development, but finds it difficult to identify the right product with the right risk-return profile. “Which is interesting, or rather a bit disappointing, because we have the capital and we would like to invest to build those houses, but we can’t make it work,” he said. For every new development APG backs, it rejects six to 10 of them. Tiedema echoed this sentiment, saying working in the Netherlands as an international investor requires “a thick skin.” Hines manages capital for the Netherlands, Germany and the Nordic countries, and all three compete for the same pool of capital. With these markets looking more attractive at the moment, Tiedema said the Dutch market is a difficult sell. However, the Netherlands only has “to make a few changes to be relatively more attractive” than the countries surrounding it, Foortse said, as the aforementioned countries face their own struggles. Among those changes needed in the Netherlands? Political stability. The Dutch cabinet nearly fell apart last week after the VVD clashed with D66 and CDA over a proposed reform of the Box 3 wealth tax system. VVD leader Dilan Yeşilgöz threatened to withdraw from the minority coalition, but after four days of crisis talks, Prime Minister Rob Jetten reached an agreement to keep the cabinet, highlighting the fragile state of the government. “Every time we meet with the ministry, we say, ‘Can we please have some stability and predictability,’ because that makes it so much easier for international investors to invest because it will just lower their return hurdle,” Foortse said. “Effectively changing the policy increases risk, and increasing risk raises your discount rates. It’s so simple, and if you maintain stability, return requirements go lower.” A major blocker for both international and domestic investors is Dutch transfer tax, which does not exist in most European countries of a similar size. For commercial properties, the transfer tax is 10.4%. Edge CEO Boudewijn Ruitenburg said a developer who buys an end-of-life building, renovates it and then sells it pays the tax twice. “It’s just ridiculous. Business cases do not work. That is something that the government needs to solve.” Ruitenburg said. At the end of the day, what international investors are looking for is very simple, said Jan-Willem Bastijn , head of EMEA transactions at CBRE Investment Management . And the fix is within reach. “They are looking for relative value. And where can I find the best value from a risk-return perspective? items.title: U.S. Industrial Leasing Tied To Data Centers Surges To 50M SF
items.description: The rapid build-out of artificial intelligence infrastructure has not only spurred unprecedented development in the data center real estate sector, but it is also increasingly supporting the industrial sector in markets across the U.S. Through the first nine months of this year, industrial tenants supporting data center development and operations signed 50M SF of deals, far surpassing the full-year totals for 2024 and 2025, according to a new report from Cushman & Wakefield . Courtesy of Cushman & Wakefield Cushman & Wakefield's report found data center-related industrial leasing is growing and making up a larger share of overall industrial demand. These tenants are bolstering the supply chains needed to build and run data centers. Cushman found three types of tenants leasing the most space: third-party logistics providers using distribution space for data center equipment, building suppliers using warehouses for data center construction materials, and manufacturers of data center equipment storing inventory in digital infrastructure hubs. These data center-related industrial tenants made up 14% of all industrial leasing last quarter and 11% through the first nine months of the year, Cushman found — up from less than 3% in 2022 and 2023 and roughly 5% in 2024 and 2025. This industrial demand surge is supporting the 36 gigawatts of data center capacity under construction in the U.S., in addition to the 47 GW of operational capacity, according to the report. It says the associated supply chain has exploded this year, with imports of AI-related equipment growing 62% from last year to $659B. “Data center development is creating a physical supply chain that extends well beyond the campus itself,” Jason Price , Cushman & Wakefield's head of Americas logistics and industrial research, said in a statement. “Servers, power and cooling equipment, construction materials and replacement parts all have to be manufactured, stored and distributed, and that is now showing up as a meaningful new source of industrial leasing.” The firm said this trend is especially prevalent in the established data center markets of Phoenix, Atlanta, Dallas-Fort Worth and Columbus, Ohio. And it is occurring in emerging data center markets like Kansas City, Austin-San Antonio, West Texas and Reno, Nevada. An industrial market report from JLL last month found overall U.S. leasing was up 38.5% year-over-year in Q3 — the highest quarter in four years — and was driven by logistics facilities supporting data centers. This activity has been driven by some of the biggest names in the AI sector. Amazon Web Services in September launched a partnership with logistics company Kuehne+Nagel to use its network to support the construction of new facilities, plus maintenance and expansion projects. Cushman said this partnership, in addition to a data center-related expansion from DHL , has helped drive industry leasing activity from third-party logistics firms. Fluidstack, an AI firm partnering with Anthropic on its data center expansion, signed a lease in June for an industrial park spanning more than 1M SF in Glendale, Arizona. Nvidia in March announced a partnership with Corning, which makes connectivity equipment for data centers, to develop three manufacturing facilities in Texas and North Carolina. “This partnership is proof that AI is not just a technology story. It is a manufacturing story, and it is happening here in the United States,” Corning CEO Wendell Weeks said in a March release on the deal. items.title: Inside Elizabeth Holmes’ Secret Oceanfront Rental Seen in ‘You Can See Everything’ Documentary a Month Before She’s Sent to Prison
items.description: The Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” takes place in the Theranos founder’s former Del Mar, CA , rental—and the property’s location in an exclusive, gated community could be just part of the reason the film’s unexpected release was such a smash. The project—which is now available to stream on demand and was directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim —was kept secret for the four years it was in production, leaving viewers in awe after the documentary’s surprise Sept. 6 premiere at Telluride Film Festival. Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans , invited the film crew—which Oppenheim told Variety was intentionally kept intimate to keep the project a secret—to reside in the guesthouse of the home for the 34 days before she reported to Federal Prison Camp in Bryan, TX , on May 30, 2023. “Keeping it under wraps was very important because we never wanted to get in front of what we were capturing,” the director shared. The crew would typically shoot for 16-hour days, with Fielder telling Variety that cameras were strategically positioned to “cover the whole house” so nothing would be missed. Loading... Directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim worked tirelessly to keep the film's creation "under wraps." JC Olivera/Getty Images Loading... The documentary takes place in Elizabeth Holmes' ultraprivate rental in an exclusive and gated community in Del Mar, CA. Google Earth Loading... The community has only about a dozen residences and is guarded around the clock. Google Earth The four-bedroom, four-bathroom beachfront property is located in an ultraprivate community less than a half-hour from San Diego . Called Sandy Lane, it features just about a dozen residences. “This is basically a hidden community. It’s a guard-gated community, which is so rare on a beach, which is why you have a lot of high-profile individuals up and down this strip,” celebrity real estate agent Josh Altman explained in a home tour of another property on the community’s sole street. Given the home's private location—and considering California ’s anti-paparazzi legislation protecting private property from capture—it’s plain to see why Holmes and Evans opted to rent the 2,200-square-foot dwelling in the time leading up to her imprisonment. The New York Times also previously reported that the couple and their two children moved to the area to be nearer to Evans’ family. His parents, William L. Evans and Susan Evans , are the hotel magnates behind Evans Hotels, a San Diego–based hospitality company. Although the property is currently off-market, a previous listing indicates the single-story home was built in 1948 and includes direct access to the private beach. Loading... Fielder and his crew were invited to live in the rental property's guesthouse for the 34 days leading up to Holmes' imprisonment. A24 Films Loading... As seen in the documentary, the midcentury-style beach abode features lots of wood paneling. A24 Films Loading... It has been reported that Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, chose to live in San Diego to be nearer his family. A24 Films Loading... Cameras were placed throughout the home to capture every moment. A24 Films Loading... Together, Holmes and Evans welcomed two children, who now reside in Texas while she serves her sentence. A24 Films As seen in the film, the abode features tall ceilings with exposed-beams and sizable windows connecting the home to the serene surrounding landscape. Midcentury modern design is present throughout the home, which is paneled in honey-hued wood. While Realtor.com® estimates the property’s current market value to be about $5.8 million, it’s unclear just how much Holmes and Evans shelled out to reside there temporarily. The most recent publicly listed rent was $5,650 a month in 2015, which is a decrease from the $5,950 rent it was listed for in 2012. The Sandy Lane spot is not the only prominent rental property Holmes has retreated to since her legal troubles began. During her trial from Aug. 31, 2021, to Jan. 3, 2022, she resided in one of the seven homes of San Francisco’s notable Green Gables. The sprawling 74-acre property was owned by the Fleishhacker family for over a century before it was sold for a record-breaking $85 million in 2025. Before Theranos came crumbling down, Holmes and her former business and romantic partner, Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani , purchased a $9 million French provincial manor in Atherton, a wealthy enclave of Silicon Valley . Privacy was likely a factor in that decision, as well, as the five-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom mansion was set behind a gated entrance and tall trees. The home was considerably more lavish than the beach bungalow that serves as the backdrop for “You Can See Everything,” with a 6,800-square-foot main home accompanied by gardens, a pool, and a pavilion on a 1.16-acre lot. Along with the couple’s young children, Evans has since relocated from California to Texas , so the family can visit Holmes in prison, where she is serving an 11-year sentence for three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The sentence was reduced to nine years for good behavior, and Holmes has since been approved for placement in a community correction center, ABC News reported , citing an update from the Department of Justice's Victim Notification System. Holmes is scheduled to be placed in the Austin Transitional Center in De Valle, TX , in August 2027. items.title: Jessica Alba Ordered To Pay Cash Warren $577K—Inside Her Recent Beverly Hills Real Estate Moves
items.description: Jessica Alba ’s divorce from Cash Warren is back in the headlines after a new court order awarded Warren $577,481 from Alba’s retirement benefits. The ruling comes after the former couple sold their longtime Beverly Hills –area home and Alba later purchased another property in the area. The retirement award comes from Alba’s account in the HonorBar Inc. Profit Sharing Plan, according to court documents reported by TMZ . Any money left in the account after Warren receives his share is to go to Alba. The documents also allow Warren to take the award as a lump sum or move it into an individual retirement account or another retirement plan. The court order also addresses account records: If Warren requests statements in writing within the next year, Alba must provide them within 10 days. Loading... Taylor Hill/Getty Images According to the outlet, transferring the money into a retirement account could avoid a 20% tax withholding. The ruling is the latest financial development following the couple’s divorce, which was finalized in February 2026. It was previously reported that Alba was ordered to pay Warren $3 million to balance the division of their assets. Their settlement also divided interests in several companies, shares in The Honest Company, and residuals from projects made during their marriage. Meanwhile, Alba and Warren have already put their real estate ties behind them. Their former Beverly Hills–area home was sold in 2025. Alba and Warren purchased the seven-bedroom estate for $9.9 million in 2017, then put it on the market in April 2025 for $18.99 million. It was sold for $18.2 million, with the closing recorded on June 27, 2025. The property sat on about 1.86 acres and included 8.5 bathrooms, a guesthouse, a home theater, and extensive grounds. Alba and Warren undertook an 18-month renovation after buying it, with Alba involved in decisions about the home’s design. The estate had been a family residence for years, and Alba spoke about the family’s plans for the house during a 2019 Architectural Digest tour. After the sale, Alba picked up a splashy Beverly Hills estate in September 2025 for $4.75 million. Loading... items.title: Derek Hough Recalls Difficult Utah Upbringing with Neighbors Who ‘Terrorized’ Family Before Moving to London
items.description: Derek Hough is opening up about his upbringing, sharing painful details from his childhood in his new Hulu documentary, “The Symphony of Dance.” In the film, the “Dancing with the Stars" judge returns to his childhood home in Utah , and details the challenging environment he was raised in. “The neighborhood that we grew up in, we definitely just had some neighbors that weren’t great,” Derek, 41, explained. “They pretty much terrorized my family in a lot of ways.” “They hung me up in a tree by my ankles. They put a gun to my head, spat on me, hogtied me up in a field and left me there,” he continued. “One of my neighbors was, for lack of a better word, really inappropriate with me, physically.” Eventually, Derek’s parents separated, and the family moved across town to an apartment building where his mother and father lived in units across the hall from one another. Loading... Derek Hough is opening up about his challenging childhood in the new Hulu documentary, "The Symphony of Dance." Disney via Getty Images Loading... The biographical film unpacks Derek's past, as well as wife Hayley Erbert Hough's life-changing brain injury. Disney via Getty Images “I remember moving away from there and feeling relieved,” he said. However, the move didn’t solve all of his problems, and he continued to struggle in the wake of his parents’ divorce. “I just didn’t understand where I was going. I didn’t understand what I was doing,” he said. “I was just kind of left to my own devices as a 12-year-old. I would skip school. I would skip dance, just floating around with no direction.” Although he had initially pushed back when his parents wanted to enroll him in dance classes, Derek explained that the artform eventually became his “safe haven”—and his ticket to a new life in London . When renowned dancers Corky and Shirley Ballas —who “Dancing with the Stars” fans will recognize as the parents of pro Mark Ballas —visited Derek’s dance studio, they saw that he had something special. “We saw the gift, we saw the talent, and we saw the struggle that his family was having at the time,” Shirley recalled in her documentary interview. “But more than that, he showed his dedication to the art. You could see it from a very, very young age.” Shirley explained that this potential is what motivated the Ballas family to take Derek under their wings. “He needed an opportunity. He needed a place to grow. And I remember him walking in, after the end of one of the classes, and saying to me, ‘Can I come and live with you?’” Shirley said. “We spoke to [his father] Bruce, he thought that was a good idea for Derek to live with us in London for a short space of time.” Loading... At just 12 years old, Derek moved to London to live with the Ballas family and focus on his dancing career. Disney via Getty Images Loading... The arrangement was only supposed to last six months, but was quickly extended, with sister Julianne Hough joining months later. Disney via Getty Images The arrangement—in which Derek was enrolled in the Italia Conti Performing Arts Academy with Mark—was initially planned to last just six months. But Derek’s father said that by Christmas of that year, the Ballas family suggested bringing sister Julianne Hough over, too. At the time, Julianne was 10 and Derek was 12. “I felt like moving away was great because I was getting away from something,” Derek explained. “I was leaving like, this wounded boy, and I was going to go become this success. I was gonna work hard and achieve things and overcome things.” The stay kept getting extended as Derek became more dedicated to ballroom dancing. “I every year, sort of begged them to come home, and they begged to stay,” Bruce said of his children’s move to London. Derek and Julianne felt very at home overseas, however. “It was almost like this ritual. Every summer we would go home, and my dad was like, ‘Yo, it’s time to come home, You guys. I wanna raise you. You’re my kids. I want you to be here,” Derek said. “And it was honestly this fight where I was like, ‘We’re on this path, and I’m gonna win this championship if I keep going here and going in this direction.” Derek would ultimately stay in London—and win a handful of titles—until 2007, when he returned to the United States full time and joined the cast of “Dancing with the Stars.” Get real estate news in your inbox Sign up now Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. Published Nov. 24, 2026 Julie Strupp Senior Editor Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print Add us on Google Getty Images There has been a flurry of national housing policy activity over the past two months. HUD recently made several changes to key programs, including launching an “express lane” for Low-Income Housing Tax Credit multifamily construction loans and making build-to-rent projects eligible for Federal Housing Administration financing. Meanwhile, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing law is now starting to be implemented . HUD and other agencies established a framework to streamline environmental review , regulation and inspection standards for housing projects. The agency also released an action plan that updates development standards for manufactured housing . The midterm results indicate more change ahead, even as housing remains a priority for both parties. To that end, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, which could speed up housing development, continues to advance through Congress . items.description:
November 23, 2026
Submitted electronically via www.regulations.gov
U.S. Department of the Treasury
Office of Capital Markets
Attention: Ethan Fallang
1500 Pennsylvania Avenue NW
Washington, DC 20220

       Re: Restrictions on Large Institutional Investor Purchases of Single-Family Homes —
       Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act Prohibition on
       Large Institutional Investor Purchases of Single-Family Homes, 31 CFR Part 36 (Docket
       No. TREAS-DO-2026-0529; RIN 1505-AC96)
Dear Deputy Assistant Secretary Fallang:
The National Rental Home Council (“NRHC”) welcomes the opportunity to provide comments
in response to the Department of the Treasury’s (“Treasury”) proposed rule implementing
Section 1001 of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (the “Act”).
The NRHC is a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit trade association that serves as the leading
voice for the single-family rental and build-to-rent housing industry. NRHC’s members include
owners, operators, and builders in the single-family rental (“SFR”) and build-to-rent (“BTR”)
housing industry, ranging from small local operators to large institutional providers of
professionally managed rental housing. The NRHC is dedicated to raising the standards for rental
housing, advancing access to high-quality single-family homes, particularly in areas where the
high cost of homeownership limits residents’ housing options, and developing and sharing best
practices throughout the single-family rental industry. Through advocacy, policy engagement,
and public education, the NRHC works to ensure that professionally managed rental home
providers can contribute to housing security, resident well-being, and the vitality of the
communities they serve.
NRHC thanks Treasury for publishing the proposed rule on an expedited timeline. Our members
appreciate your thoughtful approach and commitment to clarify open questions surrounding
Section 1001, and we look forward to working with you to ensure the final rule promotes a
strong and healthy rental marketplace for the residents our member companies serve.
 The proposal reflects a careful reading of the statute, a genuine effort to minimize market
disruption as the Act directs, and a recognition that market participants need clear, objective, and
administrable rules in order to plan, invest, and comply in a manner that advances the Act’s
overarching goal of expanding housing options and opportunities for American families. Our
comments build on that approach but recommend a series of targeted revisions that reflect
Congress’ goal underlying the Act.
NRHC’s comments are guided by a simple premise: the nation faces a severe shortage of
housing, and of quality, affordable housing in particular. Congress did not prohibit institutional

 investment in single-family homes outright; it paired the purchase prohibition with a set of
excepted purchases designed to increase housing supply, improve the quality of the existing
housing stock, and create pathways to homeownership. Those goals will be achieved only if the
exceptions are workable in practice.
Congress also directed Treasury to issue regulations that “minimize market disruptions” and
“mitigate, to the extent possible, negative impacts on consumers and communities.” NRHC
therefore urges Treasury to finalize the exceptions in a manner that limits unnecessary
impediments and encourages participation. 1




1

relevant questions presented by Treasury, describes the proposal and the issues it raises, sets out the approach
NRHC urges Treasury to consider, and proposes revisions to the regulatory text, which are shown in blue underlined
text and proposed deletions in red struck-through text.



                           NRHC: Treasury Road to Housing Comment Letter | Page 2 of 25

   A. Relevant Questions Presented

Question 25: Is the proposed definition appropriately tailored to identify purchases made
pursuant to build-to-rent programs? Should the definition provide additional terms relating to
single-family homes that a large institutional investor constructs or constructs and retains?

Question 32: Are the proposed conditions for no prior owner-occupancy and purchases within
18 months appropriate and administrable indicators for determining whether a home is newly
constructed? What alternatives should Treasury consider to either or both of these factors?

Question 34: Is 18 months after the certificate of occupancy (or equivalent) an appropriate
period of time for determining whether a single-family home is newly constructed?

Question 37: Should the rule be revised to reflect circumstances in which a single-family home is
held unoccupied by a large institutional investor after the purchase, before being occupied by a
renter?

NRHC respectfully concludes that Section 1001(a)(2)(B) of the Act, which establishes the
“build-to-rent” (“BTR”) excepted purchase category, does not support Treasury’s 18-month test
in proposed Section 36.5. Treasury should remove this artificial timeline test in keeping with
Congress’ intent and the overall purpose of the statute.

                   FEDERAL HOUSING FINANCE AGENCY

For Immediate Release                                       Contact:    MediaInquiries@FHFA.GOV
November 24, 2026

                  U.S. House Prices Rise 2.5 Percent Year over Year;
                        Up 0.7 percent Quarter over Quarter
Washington, D.C. – U.S. house prices rose 2.5 percent between the third quarter of 2025 and the
third quarter of 2026, according to the U.S. Federal Housing (FHFA) House Price Index (FHFA
HPI®). House prices for the third quarter of 2026 rose 0.7 percent compared to the second quarter
of 2026. FHFA’s seasonally adjusted monthly index for September remained unchanged from
August.

Significant Findings
   Nationally, the U.S. housing market has experienced positive annual appreciation each quarter
    since the start of 2012.
   House prices rose in 48 states between the third quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026.
    The five states with the highest annual appreciation were 1) Alaska, 8.2 percent; 2)
    Connecticut, 5.4 percent; 3) Wisconsin, 5.3 percent; 4) Indiana, 5.3 percent; and 5) North
    Dakota, 5.2 percent. District of Columbia recorded a 4.2 percent price decline.
   House prices rose in 82 of the 100 largest metropolitan areas over the previous four quarters.
    The annual price increase was the greatest in Greensboro-High Point, NC, at 8.9 percent. The
    metropolitan area that experienced the most significant price decline was Washington, DC-MD
    at 4.9 percent.
   All nine census divisions had positive house price changes year-over-year. The Middle
    Atlantic division recorded the strongest appreciation, posting a 4.9 percent increase from the
    third quarter of 2025 to the third quarter of 2026. The Pacific division recorded a 0.5 percent
    price increase.
   Trends in the Top 100 Metropolitan Statistical Areas are available in our interactive dashboard:
    https://www.fhfa.gov/data/dashboard/fhfa-hpi-top-100-metro-area-rankings. The first tab
    displays rankings, and the second tab offers charts.

The FHFA HPI is a comprehensive collection of publicly available house price indexes that tracks
changes in single-family home values across the United States. The data extend back to the mid-
1970s and cover all 50 states and more than 400 American cities. Drawing on information from
over 100 million home sales and refinance transactions, the FHFA HPI provides detailed insights
into house price trends at the national, census division, state, metropolitan area, county, ZIP code,
                                                   -1-
 and census tract levels. FHFA employs a transparent, weighted repeat-sales methodology to
measure changes in home prices using historical housing transaction data.

FHFA releases HPI data and reports quarterly and monthly. The flagship FHFA HPI uses seasonally
adjusted, purchase-only data from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Additional indexes use other data,
including refinances, mortgages insured by the Federal Housing Administration, and real property
records. All the indexes (including their historic values) and information about future HPI release
dates are available on FHFA’s website: https://www.fhfa.gov/HPI.

Tables and graphs showing home price statistics for metropolitan areas, states, census divisions, and
the United States are included on the following pages.

Class A assets are trading at a median price of $491,300 per unit with cap rates closer to 5.0%. This balance between supply and demand has yielded steady operational conditions throughout much of Greater Los Angeles, although there has been some varied performance in the major geographic segments of the region. The South Bay has led the way, while the San Fernando Valley and West Los Angeles submarkets have closely tracked the larger market trend of stable performance. Conditions have continued to soften in Downtown Los Angeles in response to a supply-demand imbalance. items.title: The 1-million-dollar question
items.description: Record-level wealth has accumulated in properties across the globe. But accessing that wealth has become a pricey proposition. Capital gains taxes increasingly burden homeowners and investors, dissuading many from selling and contributing to the stagnation of global property markets. One in 12 U.S. sellers now pay capital gains tax on profits from selling a primary residence — that’s a seven-percentage point jump from the early 2010s, according to Cotality analysis. In Australia, it’s investors who pay capital gains taxes, and there these taxes are poised to rise materially as policies are revised next year. These taxes have had a hand in slowing global markets. U.S. homeowners hold onto property for an average of 11.9 years. In Australia, that figure is 9 years. Ten years ago, those numbers were 9.6 and 8.4 years, respectively. Housing ties up over one-quarter of American wealth. For those under 40, it’s over a third of their net worth. Archana Pradan Principal Economist, Cotality Midway to the goal The housing market remains a focal point in the U.S. as mid-term elections approach. Both sides of the aisle support tax breaks for homeowners who realize net proceeds of $1 million or less. The line of thinking points to larger tax breaks incentivizing sales. According to Cotality data, adjusting tax thresholds is one way to move markets. In the U.S., adjusting the current $500,000 tax exclusion set in 1997 to $1,000,000 would reduce the number of homeowners paying property gains taxes by nearly three-quarters. That means millions of homeowners would be free to collect their profits, invest in new homes, and turn over their old properties to new homeowners. “Housing ties up over one-quarter of American wealth. For those under 40, it’s over a third of their net worth,” said Archana Pradhan, principal economist at Cotality. “While equity gains have stabilized the U.S. economy, it also means that taxes can consume a larger share of someone’s net wealth. That reality gives people pause before they sell.” The long game There is a direct link between the size of realized equity gains and homeownership periods. Cotality data show that in the U.S., as the share of sales exceeding the current $500,000 tax exemption set in 1997 climbed, so did the average length of time someone owned a home. ‍ Tracking the relationship between homeownership and capital gains taxes Year Share of sales exceeding 500k Average time as homeowner whose capital gains 2020 2.7% 16.6 years 2021 5.1% 15.9 years 2022 6.8% 15.5 years 2023 6.5% 16.7 years 2024 7.8% 17.1 years 2025 8.1% 17.8 years 2026 7.5% 18.4 years Data source: Cotality, 2026 People can hold onto homes to avoid triggering tax and financing penalties. Some entirely circumvent capital gains taxes in the U.S. by using inheritance to transition ownership. Cotality analysis showed that a record 7% of all property transfers came through inheritance. In California, where 25% of homes sold require owners to pay capital gains taxes, homes are inherited at twice the rate seen in the rest of the country. This approach further stymies market movement. When natural housing turnover stalls, choice is limited, profits remain unrealized, and people’s finances and market demands can diverge. Australia’s interest in investment The pattern of high taxes deterring home sales is a part of the Australian market conversation as well. Already, the length of time people own a home has increased, but new taxation laws are positioned to push those numbers higher. Recently, the Australian government revised the rules for home investors. Now, instead of receiving a 50% discount on the marginal tax rate for profits realized when selling, gains will be taxed using a CPI indexation method . “There is widespread speculation that these changes will act as disincentive for investment activity across Australian housing,” said Tim Lawless, Cotality’s Head of Research in Australia. “It may also incentivize investors holding onto their properties for longer.” The affordability gap in Australia has been widening for years and slowing the traditional trade-up cycle. Homeowners in the country hold their properties for an average of nine years, but it's not because no one wants to buy a home. In a recent survey from Cotality , 75% of Aussie buyers said they are willing to reduce spending and accept the highest interest rates of any country surveyed. If investors start to feel the squeeze and respond by holding onto their properties for longer, that could further limit available inventor across an already tightly supplied market. The ones who pay the price will be the homeowners whose budgets are already under strain. See more Track home prices across the U.S. Step up on the ladder Homeownership is an increasingly expensive proposition. Elevated interest rates and ballooning insurance costs and taxes — from both property taxes and capital gains — have coincided with decreasing application volumes. Cotality data shows that when interest rates moved from 4.5% in January 2019 to 6.9% in January 2025, lenders wrote almost 1 million fewer loans. Still, would-be buyers are trying to make homeownership work. In Cotality’s recent survey of recent and future homebuyers, it is clear that there is an order in which people are willing to make sacrifices to own a home.
